Her Majesty the Queen v. Harding

[Indexed as: R. v. Harding]

52 O.R. (3d) 714

[2001] O.J. No. 325

Court File No. 22-99

Ontario Superior Court of Justice

Dambrot J.

January 31, 2001

Criminal law--Promoting hatred--Accused wrote and distributed pamphlets and telephone messages promoting hatred of Muslims --Accused convicted--Accused alleging judge erring in holding wilful blindness satisfying Charter requirements for mens rea and for holding defence in
s. 319(3)
(b) of
Criminal Code
not available to accused--Trial judge correct--Accused cannot rely on s. 319(3)(b) to intermingle messages promoting hatred with protected religious comment--Appeal dismissed --Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1, 2(b)--
Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 319(2)
, (3)(b).

Charter of Rights
and Freedoms--Freedom of expression --Accused writing and distributing hate propaganda against Muslims--Trial judge finding accused at least wilfully blind to promotion of hatred arising from pamphlets and telephone messages--Wilful blindness meeting requirements for mens rea pursuant to s. 7 of Charter--Trial judge correctly finding that accused not entitled to rely on defence in
s. 319(3)
(b) of
Criminal Code
because protected religious comment was wilfully intermixed with messages promoting hatred--Appeal from conviction dismissed--Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1, 2, 7--Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 319.
The accused was convicted of wilful promotion of hatred contrary to
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
. He expressed the views, in pamphlets and a telephone message, that Muslims, as a group, are dangerous people, capable of acts of violent terrorism and cruelty; that they pose a threat to other faiths and that it is the objective of Canadian Muslims to overtake the country. The trial judge found that the accused wilfully promoted hatred or was at least wilfully blind to the fact that the promotion of hatred was a substantially certain consequence of his acts. The trial judge also held that the defence in s. 319(3)(b) of the Code, which entitles an accused to an acquittal where it is established that the accused, in good faith, expressed or attempted to establish by argument an opinion on a religious subject, was not applicable. The trial judge found that the intermingling of references to atrocities being committed by Muslim terrorists abroad with the accused's religious opinions, coupled with his statements that all Muslims in Canada are the same as those committing the atrocities, was intended to convey a message above and beyond religious opinion: that is, that Muslims in Canada are dangerous and are to be feared. The accused appealed, arguing that wilful blindness falls short of the strict mens rea requirements that are necessary in order for the limits on freedom of speech in
s. 319(2)
to be justified under
s. 1
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
; and that the trial judge erred in interpreting the defence in s. 319(3)(b) narrowly.
Held, the appeal should be dismissed.
Wilful blindness, unlike recklessness, is a purely subjective form of mens rea, and is equivalent to knowledge. To be wilfully blind, an accused must suspect a fact, realize its probability, and refrain from obtaining the final confirmation, wanting to be able to deny knowledge. Wilful blindness is a constitutionally sufficient mens rea for the offence of promoting hatred. If the trial judge in fact convicted the accused on the basis of wilful blindness, he did not err in doing so.
The trial judge found that, while the offensive statements were intermingled with protected religious opinion, they were, nonetheless, separate false allegations about Muslims calculated to arouse fear and hatred in non-Muslim people. Accordingly, unless the defence in s. 319(3)(b) is intended to protect statements that promote hatred against an identifiable group merely because the statements are located within a larger statement that also contains an expression of opinion on a religious subject, there was no basis to interfere with the trial judge's conclusion that the defence was not available to the accused. There was no reason to read s. 319(3)(b) as affording such protection as they can only rationally provide a defence to a person who, by communicating statements other than in private conversation, wilfully promotes hatred against an identifiable group, in the rare circumstances where, in the communication of those very statements, that person, in good faith, was expressing or att empting to establish by an argument an opinion on a religious subject. There is no reason to construe the defence in s. 319(3)(b) in a manner that would permit the mere imbedding of a wilful message of hate within protected religious comment to immunize the maker of the message from successful prosecution.
APPEAL from a judgment of Linden C. Prov. J. (1998),
1998 CanLII 18857 (ON CTGD)
, 45 O.R. (3d) 207 (Prov. Ct.).

Peter Van Den Bergh, for respondent.
Peter R. Jervis and Jasmine T. Akbarali, for appellant.

[
1
] DAMBROT J.:--The appellant was convicted by Chief Judge
Linden of the Ontario Court (Provincial Division) in Toronto on
June 19, 1998 of three counts of wilful promotion of hatred
contrary to
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code [R.S.C. 1985, c. C-
46
]. In R. v. Keegstra,
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, 61 C.C.C. (3d)
1, the Supreme Court unanimously concluded that the offence
created by
s. 319(2)
restricts the freedom of expression
guaranteed by
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
. The court nevertheless upheld the constitutional
validity of this provision under
s. 1
of the Charter. In doing
so, the majority of the court emphasized those features of the
offence that minimize the impairment of freedom of expression,
and limit the incursion of
s. 319(2)
into the realm of
acceptable, albeit offensive or controversial, expression. On
this appeal from his conviction, the appellant argues that in
convicting him, the learned trial judge overstepped the
constitutional boundaries of
s. 319(2)
and punished him for
disseminating acceptable expression.

[
2
] In addition to his appeal from conviction, the appellant
initially appealed the concurrent conditional three-month
sentences imposed by Linden C. Prov. J. on each count, followed
by two years' probation. He subsequently abandoned that aspect
of his appeal. The Crown, however, has maintained a sentence
appeal.

The Facts

[
3
] Between April 30 and June 24, 1997 the appellant wrote
and distributed two pamphlets entitled Let's Take a Serious
Look at What's Happening to Western Collegiate High School and
Are all the Muslims living in Canada today terrorsits (sic):
This is a warning to all Canadians and their families. As well,
he created a telephone message that he invited members of the
public to hear. This communication clearly conveyed a warning
that Canadian-Muslims are a part of a worldwide conspiracy that
poses a threat to the security and well-being of Canadians.

[
4
] Specifically, in "Let's Take a Serious Look at What's
Happening to Western Collegiate . . ." the appellant:

--  after describing incidents of horrific violence perpetrated
by radical Muslim militants in other parts of the world,
comments that there is "no difference in the Muslims living
here or anywhere else in the world";

--  describes Muslims as "violent and hateful towards Jews,
Christians and anyone else that denies or objects to their
false religion";

--  states that Muslims masquerade as pacifists "but underneath
their false sheep's clothing are raging wolves, seeking
whom they may devour and Toronto is definitely on their hit
list";

--  suggests that there is a Muslim conspiracy to take over Canada;
Canada [and]

--  describes the Muslim religion as "full of hate and violence"
and posing a "threat to our children".

[
5
] In "Are all the Muslims living in Canada today terrorsits
[sic] . . ." the appellant:

--  again cites incidents of violent atrocities committed by
"Muslim terrorists" and then states that "we have the
same Muslim believers living right here in Toronto";

--  states his intention to "cry out to Canadians to warn them
about all Muslims";

--  states that "the objective of every Muslim living in this
city" is to take over and make Canada into a Muslim country;

--  states that although the Muslims in this city are outwardly
peaceful, in truth they are "like raging wolves in sheep's
clothing, inside they are full of hate, violence and
murder";

--  suggests that Muslims are incapable of living peacefully
among non-Muslims in Canada because their mandate is to turn
Canada into a Muslim society and, as proven by acts
committed in other parts of the world, they will use
violence to achieve their ends; [and]

--  invites his readers to help to "stand in the way of Muslim
believers whose only wish is to control by their religion
and to punish anyone they can't control".

[
6
] In the telephone message, the appellant repeats the
themes in the pamphlets, referring to acts of violent cruelty
committed by Muslims in other parts of the world "in the name
of their God" and stating that "the Muslims living in Toronto
are no different".

The Judgment of Chief Judge Linden

[
7
] In his cogent, clear and comprehensive reasons for
judgment, Linden C. Prov. J. concluded that the Crown was
obliged to establish the following:

(a) that the appellant communicated statements;

(b) that the statements were communicated other than in private
conversation;

(c) that the statements promoted hatred;

(d) that the promotion of hatred was against an identifiable
group; and

(e) that the appellant did so wilfully.

[
8
] Linden C. Prov. J. had little difficulty in quickly
concluding that items (a) and (b) had been established. After
noting that, for reasons that would be discussed later in the
judgment, he found that the two pamphlets and the first
telephone message clearly promoted hatred, he further indicated
that he was satisfied that item (d) had been established. I
note that none of items (a), (b) and (d) were truly in issue.

[
9
] Linden C. Prov. J. then instructed himself in
considerable detail on the meaning of "wilful" and the
requisite mens rea of this offence as explained by Dickson
C.J.C. in Keegstra, as well as the meaning of "hatred". He then
proceeded to consider item (c), that is, whether the Crown had
established that the appellant's statements promoted hatred. He
began by summarizing [at p. 213 O.R.] the contents of the
pamphlets and the telephone message as follows:

(a) The prevailing theme is that Muslims as a group are
dangerous people capable of acts of violent terrorism and
great cruelty.

(b) Muslims are intolerant of other faiths and pose a threat to
such groups. In particular, they are rabidly anti-Semitic
and anti-Christian.

(c) Muslims have perpetrated horrific acts of violent terrorism
throughout the world in the name of their religion.

(d) Canadian Muslims are no different from their brethren in
other countries, but they dishonestly masquerade as
pacifists. They are "like raging wolves in sheep's
clothing, inside they are full of hate, violence, and
murder."

(e) It is the objective of all Canadian Muslims to overtake
this country. A "holy war" is being waged. When Muslims
succeed with this goal, they will brutalize those who do
not accept their religion.

[
10
] He then concluded that these materials deliver a message
of hatred within the meaning of
s. 319(2)
. He said [at pp.
213-14 O.R.]:

Muslims are depicted as persons who readily commit heinous
atrocities for the sake of their religious beliefs.

Mr. Harding posits a world-wide Muslim conspiracy theory to
the effect that all Muslims are united in the goal of
overtaking the societies in which they live, and subjecting
those who do not embrace their ways to violent oppression. He
warns that Canadian Muslims are no different, but that they
deceive us as to their true nature and intentions. The clear
message is that Muslims pose a dangerous and insidious threat
to the security and well-being of Canadians.

The feelings promoted by this material amount to "the most
intense form of dislike". The logical implication of the
message conveyed is that Muslims are detestable people,
deserving of our contempt. The material targets all Muslims,
and warns the reader not to be fooled by their duplicity.

It goes further and invites the reader, in non-specific
terms, to take defensive action against the threat of
violence posed by Muslims as a group. The inevitable
conclusion is that Muslims are deserving of ill-treatment on
the basis of group-affiliation.

[
11
] After explaining why he was not satisfied beyond a
reasonable doubt that the second telephone message, although
highly offensive and distasteful, breached the section, the
trial judge turned to the mental element of the offence. He
began by saying [at p. 214 O.R.]:

In regard to the two pamphlets and the first phone message,
Mr. Harding's goal may well have been to rouse Christians to
defend and propagate their religion. That, in itself, is
neither an unworthy nor an illegal goal. His goal may also
have been to stem what he perceived to be the dangerous
spreading of Islam. That, too, is not an illegal goal.
However, the means chosen to attain that goal are found by
this court to be the unworthy and illegal means of
engendering fear of and hatred towards Muslims. Although Mr.
Harding denies having the intent to promote hatred when
disseminating his message, he was at best wilfully blind.

[
12
] Linden C. Prov. J. then reviewed the Crown's argument
that the evidence demonstrates that the promotion of hatred
brought about by the appellant's messages could not have been
accidental. The catalogue of circumstances supporting an
inference of wilfulness is lengthy and compelling. It includes,
by way of example only, evidence that the appellant distorted
the statements taken from various newspaper articles that he
purported to quote from in his statements, in an obvious effort
to obscure the distinctions made in those articles between
Muslims in general, and Muslim extremists, as well as to
distort the nature of the Muslim prayer activity permitted in
Western Collegiate; the fact that the appellant's testimony at
trial that he did not intend to disparage Muslims was not
offered to the police in his interview with them at the time of
their investigation -- rather, he attempted to explain and
justify his statements to the police; that his claim at trial
that he did not understand what it was about the statements
that concerned the police at the time of his interview,
resulting in his not providing the explanation he gave at trial
to the police was at odds with the audiotape of the interview,
which demonstrates that he was questioned directly about
specific passages in the material and asked to explain their
meaning; and the fact that he made disparaging comments about
Muslims even in his interview with the police, saying, for
example, "[T]hese people do not obey our laws, so we must teach
them to obey our laws," and "[Muslims] believe that the Islamic
-- that the Koran must take over the world. That is their
ultimate goal." [At p. 217 O.R.]

[
13
] Linden C. Prov. J. concluded [at pp. 217-18 O.R.] that
the appellant had the requisite intent to commit the offence.
He stated:

To find that Mr. Harding did not have the requisite intent
to commit this offence, the court would have to accept, or
reasonably doubt, that the powerful web of inculpatory
circumstances in which Mark Harding found himself were all
just a horrible coincidence. I'm referring now to the oral
submissions of Ms. Klukach, that he simply missed the
painfully obvious meaning of what he was writing. That he
innocently altered and materially misrepresented newspaper
articles in a manner that just coincidentally happened to
further the very message that he says he did not appreciate
that he was conveying. That he changed his telephone message
when told to tone it down in a manner that just
coincidentally removed his generalized attack on all Muslims,
even though he did not actually appreciate that that was the
meaning that those words were conveying. That in spite of his
professed sincere concern, and strong interest in this issue,
he showed no real interest in engaging in a public dialogue
about it, turning down the offer of Shabir Ally to publicly
debate his concerns about the Islamic faith. That despite the
obvious anger, and impatience evinced in his telephone
contacts and correspondence with Islamic organizations, after
they rebuffed his efforts to convert them, he harboured no
feelings of animus toward Muslims. That the marked change in
the tenor of his writings was really without significance.

Now, Mr. Harding offered alternative explanations for these
circumstances and placed a different gloss on each in
isolation.

However, the court agrees with the Crown's submission that
their cumulative force, and the sheer improbability of all of
this being just part of one big misunderstanding, adds up to
an overwhelming case of guilty intent.

For Mark Harding's evidence to be seen as even remotely
plausible when he told the court that he did not appreciate
what he was writing, that he did not intend to promote a
message of hate, the court would have to accept that he is
unbelievably naive and inept, himself, a victim of his own
inadvertence.

It may well be that Mark Harding now regrets his lapse in
his normal approach of Christian love and forgiveness and
that he is now somewhat shamed by it, but on the whole of the
evidence presented in this case, there is no doubt that by
communicating statements, other than in private conversation,
he wilfully promoted hatred against an identifiable group,
namely Muslims in Canada.

[
14
] Linden C. Prov. J. then went on to consider the
statutory defences contained in
s. 319(3)
of the
Criminal Code
.
He stated [at p. 219 O.R.]:

Despite the fact that this court has found beyond a
reasonable doubt that Mr. Harding did promote hatred, and did
so wilfully, it is necessary that each of the defences be
addressed separately.

(Emphasis added)

[
15
] With respect to the defence found in
s. 319(3)
(b), which
entitles an accused to an acquittal where it is established
that the accused, in good faith, expressed or attempted to
establish by argument an opinion on a religious subject, Linden
C. Prov. J. had this to say [at pp. 219-20 O.R.]:

Now, Mr. Harding is entitled to his opinions on religious
subjects, and he is entitled to publicly attempt to convince
others of the correctness of his beliefs. His pamphlets and
message do contain opinions of religious belief which he
appears to sincerely hold. Had he confined his message to
those opinions, I doubt that the Crown would have been able
to convince the court that he was thereby wilfully promoting
hatred, no matter how incorrect those beliefs may be. It is
not a crime in Canada to proclaim that a particular religion
is the only true religion, and that another religion with
conflicting beliefs is false. If that were the case, the
courts would be full of sincere believers of a variety of
faiths, and freedom of speech would not exist in Canada.

Unfortunately, religious opinions about the falseness of
Islam are not all that Mr. Harding's communications
contained. They also contain alarming and false allegations
about the adherents of Islam calculated to arouse fear and
hatred of them in all non-Muslim people, particularly
Christians. Although expression of religious opinion is
strongly protected, this protection cannot be extended to
shield this type of communication simply because they are
contained in the same message and the one is used to bolster
the other. If that were the case, religious opinion could be
used with impunity as a Trojan Horse to carry the intended
message of hate forbidden by
s. 319
. The intermingling of
references to atrocities being committed by Muslim terrorists
abroad, with Mr. Harding's religious opinions, coupled with
his statements that all Muslims in Canada are the same as
those committing the atrocities, is obviously intended to
convey a message above and beyond religious opinion; that
Muslims here are dangerous and are to be feared.

I do not think that the defence which para. (b) offers is
applicable.

[
16
] After a careful consideration of each of the remaining
defences, Linden C. Prov. J. concluded [at pp. 222-23 O.R.]:

In conclusion, after reading the material as a whole, after
listening to the witnesses and considering the submissions of
counsel, this court is convinced beyond a reasonable doubt
that Mr. Harding either intended to promote hatred towards
Muslims, or was wilfully blind that such was a substantially
certain consequence.

After consideration of the defences in
s. 319(3)
, the court
finds that none of the defences are applicable to the facts
of this case.

A paraphrase of Chief Justice Dickson's statement in the
Keegstra case is apposite. It will be a rare case where one
who intends to promote hatred will be found to be acting in
good faith, or upon honest belief. This is not one of those
cases. Accordingly, there will be a finding of guilt on
counts 1 and 2, and on count 3, in relation to the first
message.

Issues

[
17
] The appellant advanced the following grounds of appeal
in his factum:

(a) the trial judge erred in his interpretation and
application of the term "wilfully" in
s. 319(2)
of the

Criminal Code
by importing an element of "recklessness"
into the mens rea requirement, thereby diluting its
strictness and encroaching upon the constitutionally
guaranteed right to freedom of expression; and

(b) the trial judge erred in his interpretation and
application of the defence set out in
s. 319(3)
(b) of
the
Criminal Code
by interpreting it narrowly, out of
context and in violation of
Charter
values, thereby
criminalizing expression which is entitled to
constitutional protection.

[
18
] After reviewing the respondant's factum, the appellant
recognized that his first ground of appeal was misconceived.
The law is clear that wilful blindness is distinct from and
does not include an element of recklessness, but rather arises
when a person has become aware of the need for some inquiry but
declines to make the inquiry in order to avoid the truth and
remain ignorant. As a result, the appellant recast his first
ground of appeal as follows:

(a) Wilful blindness falls short of the strict mens rea
requirements of
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
, and
encroaches upon the constitutionally guaranteed right
to freedom of expression.

[
19
] I will deal with each of the grounds of appeal in turn.

Wilful Blindness

Does the issue arise?

[
20
] During oral argument, I raised an initial concern that I
had upon reading the reasons of Linden C. Prov. J. that the
issue concerning wilful blindness did not arise in this case,
having regard to his clear finding at several points in his
judgment that the appellant did wilfully promote hatred against
Muslims in Canada. The appellant responded that while the trial
judge did appear to make this finding, the language of the
judgment elsewhere reveals that he could not definitively find
that the appellant's state of mind was higher than wilful
blindness. I will consider this preliminary matter before
turning to the merits of this ground of appeal.

[
21
] To put this issue in context, I note that when he first
began to discuss the mental element of the offence in his
judgment, Linden C. Prov. J. stated [at p. 214 O.R.], "Although
Mr. Harding denies having the intent to promote hatred when
disseminating his message, he was at best wilfully blind."
After reviewing the various pieces of evidence relevant to the
issue of intent, however, he stated, "the court agrees with the
Crown's submission that their cumulative force, and the sheer
improbability of all of this being just part of one big
misunderstanding, adds up to an overwhelming case of guilty
intent." Shortly after this statement, he went on to say [at p.
218 O.R.], "on the whole of the evidence presented in this
case, there is no doubt that by communicating statements, other
than in private conversation, he wilfully promoted hatred
against an identifiable group, namely Muslims in Canada."
Before going on to consider the various statutory defences, he
stated, "Despite the fact that this court has found beyond a
reasonable doubt that Mr. Harding did promote hatred, and did
so wilfully, it is necessary that each of the defences be
addressed separately." Finally, however, after considering the
defences, he returned to his initial formulation, and stated
[at p. 222 O.R.], "this court is convinced beyond a
reasonable doubt that Mr. Harding either intended to promote
hatred towards Muslims, or was wilfully blind that such was a
substantially certain consequence."

[
22
] To summarize, Linden C. Prov. J. made a clear finding of
fact that the appellant had the intent to promote hatred, but
placed that finding between two assertions that Mr. Harding
either intended to promote hatred, or was wilfully blind to the
fact that the promotion of hatred was a substantially certain
consequence of his acts. While upon a superficial analysis of
the judgment this could appear to be contradictory, I view the
matter differently. It seems to me that whenever the mental
element of an offence is proved circumstantially, it is always
possible that despite even overwhelming evidence of intent, the
accused may have closed his or her eyes in the face of a need
to make inquiries, declined to make those inquir[ies] in order
to avoid the truth and remained ignorant. Without being able to
see into a person's mind, this alternative must exist. That is
all that Linden C. Prov. J. was saying. He did not find that
the appellant was wilfully blind; he simply could not eliminate
the remote possibility that he was. But in saying this, I
recognize that the constitutional issue raised by the appellant
cannot be avoided. If wilful blindness is not an acceptable
mental element for this offence, the fact that it can rarely be
eliminated by proof beyond a reasonable [doubt] is no answer to
the appellant's argument. Accordingly, I will proceed to
consider the issue raised by the appellant.

Is wilful blindness a constitutional mental element for the
offence of wilfully promoting hatred?

[
23
] This discussion must commence with a consideration of
the judgment of Dickson C.J.C. for the majority of the Supreme
Court of Canada in Keegstra, supra. In Keegstra, after
concluding that
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
constitutes an
infringement of the guarantee of freedom of expression found in

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
, Dickson C.J.C. went on to consider
whether the infringement was justifiable under
s. 1
as a
reasonable limit in a free and democratic society. He concluded
that it was a reasonable limit. He expressed the view that the
provision furthers an immensely important objective, is
directed at expression distant from the core of free expression
values and satisfies each of the components of the
proportionality inquiry mandated by
s. 1
.

[
24
] Of greatest pertinence to the issue here is the
discussion in the judgment of Dickson C.J.C. of whether
s.
319(2)
minimally impairs freedom of expression. He summarized
his conclusions on this issue as follows, at pp. 785-86 S.C.R.;
pp. 65-66 C.C.C.:

To summarize the above discussion, in light of the great
importance of Parliament's objective and the discounted value
of the expression at issue I find that the terms of
s. 319(2)

create a narrowly confined offence which suffers from neither
overbreadth nor vagueness. This interpretation stems largely
from my view that the provision possesses a stringent mens
rea requirement, necessitating either an intent to promote
hatred or knowledge of the substantial certainty of such, and
is also strongly supported by the conclusion that the meaning
of the word "hatred" is restricted to the most severe and
deeply-felt form of opprobrium. Additionally, however, the
conclusion that
s. 319(2)
represents a minimal impairment of
the freedom of expression gains credence through the
exclusion of private conversation from its scope, the need
for the promotion of hatred to focus upon an identifiable
group and the presence of the
s. 319(3)
defences. As for the
argument that other modes of combating hate propaganda
eclipse the need for a criminal provision, it is eminently
reasonable to utilize more than one type of legislative tool
in working to prevent the spread of racist expression and its
resultant harm. It will indeed be more difficult to justify a
criminal statute under
s. 1
, but in my opinion the necessary
justificatory arguments have been made out with respect to
s.
319(2)
.

I thus conclude that
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
does
not unduly impair the freedom of expression, and it remains
only to examine whether its effects none the less present so
grave a limitation upon the
s. 2
(b) guarantee so as to
outweigh the benefits to be gained from a measure otherwise
proportional to an important legislative objective.

[
25
] It is apparent from the foregoing that interpreting
s.
319(2)
to have a stringent mens rea requirement, necessitating
either an intent to promote hatred or knowledge of the
substantial certainty of such, is of fundamental importance to
its constitutional validity. Dickson C.J.C. elaborated on the
meaning of the word "wilfully" in this provision, placing great
emphasis on the judgment of Martin J.A. in R. v. Buzzanga
(1979),
1979 CanLII 1927 (ON CA)
, 25 O.R. (2d) 705, 49 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (C.A.), as
follows at pp. 774-75 S.C.R., pp. 57-58 C.C.C.:

On appeal, Martin J.A. overturned the conviction. He noted
that the word "wilfully" does not have a fixed meaning in
criminal law, and thus sought to divine the use and import of
the word as it appears in
s. 319(2)
(pp. 379-81). Comparing
the section with s. 319(1) (then s. 281.2(1)), which
prohibits incitement to hatred in a public place where such
incitement is likely to lead to a breach of peace, he said
(at pp. 381-2):

The insertion of the word "wilfully" in [s. 319(2)] was not
necessary, to import mens rea since that requirement would
be implied in any event because of the serious nature of
the offence: see R. v. Prue, supra. The statements, the
communication of which are proscribed by [
s. 319(2)
], are
not confined to statements communicated in a public place
in circumstances likely to lead to a breach of the peace
and they, consequently, do not pose such an immediate
threat to public order as those falling under [s. 319(1)];
it is reasonable to assume, therefore, that Parliament
intended to limit the offence under [
s. 319(2)
] to the
intentional promotion of hatred. It is evident that the use
of the word "wilfully" in [
s. 319(2)
], and not in [s.
319(1)], reflects Parliament's policy to strike a balance
in protecting the competing social interests of freedom of
expression on the one hand, and public order and group
reputation on the other hand.

More specifically, Martin J.A. went on to elaborate on the
meaning of "wilfully", concluding that this mental element is
satisfied only where an accused subjectively desires the
promotion of hatred or foresees such a consequence as certain
or substantially certain to result from an act done in order
to achieve some other purpose (pp. 384-5). On the facts in
Buzzanga, the trial judge had informed the jury that
"wilfully" could be equated with the intention to create
"controversy, furor and an uproar" (p. 386). This
interpretation was clearly incompatible with Martin J.A.'s
requirement that the promotion of hatred be intended or
foreseen as substantially certain, and a new trial was
therefore ordered.

The interpretation of "wilfully" in Buzzanga has great
bearing upon the extent to which
s. 319(2)
limits the freedom
of expression. This mental element, requiring more than
merely negligence or recklessness as to result, significantly
restricts the reach of the provision, and thereby reduces the
scope of the targeted expression.

[
26
] After noting that in some offences the element of
wilfulness can be supplied by recklessness, Martin J.A.
specifically excluded recklessness from
s. 319(2)
at p. 381 of
Buzzanga, where he stated [at p. 717 O.R.]:

As previously indicated, the word "wilfully" does not have
a fixed meaning, but I am satisfied that in the context of s.
281.2(2) it means with the intention of promoting hatred, and
does not include recklessness. The arrangement of the
legislation proscribing the incitement of hatred, in my view,
leads to that conclusion.

[
27
] It is noteworthy that while both Martin J.A. in Buzzanga
and Dickson C.J.C. in Keegstra specifically excluded
recklessness from the mental element of the offence created by

s. 319(2)
, neither jurist made any specific reference to wilful
blindness. As a result, it becomes necessary to examine closely
the nature of the concept of wilful blindness to determine
whether or not it is excluded.

[
28
] It is probably fair to say that the application of the
concept of wilful blindness has sometimes been the subject of
less than rigorous analysis in the past. The Supreme Court of
Canada brought considerable clarity to the subject in its
judgment in Sansregret v. R.,
1985 CanLII 79 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 570, 18 C.C.C.
(3d) 223. The judgment of McIntyre J. for the court places
it beyond dispute that wilful blindness, unlike recklessness,
is a purely subjective form of mens rea, and indeed is the
equivalent of knowledge. While recklessness has an element of
subjectiveness, it also has an objective dimension. To be
reckless, an accused must do something that is objectively
determined to risk bringing about a prohibited result, being
aware that his or her conduct could bring about that result.
The definition of wilful blindness, on the other hand, makes
clear that this form of intent, as I have just stated, is
purely subjective. To be wilfully blind, an accused must
suspect a fact, realize its prob ability, and refrain from
obtaining the final confirmation, wanting to be able to deny
knowledge.

[
29
] In Sansregret, McIntyre J. put the matter as follows, at
pp. 581-82 S.C.R., p. 233 C.C.C.:

The concept of recklessness as a basis for criminal
liability has been the subject of much discussion.
Negligence, the failure to take reasonable care, is a
creature of the civil law and is not generally a concept
having a place in determining criminal liability.
Nevertheless, it is frequently confused with recklessness in
the criminal sense and care should be taken to separate the
two concepts. Negligence is tested by the objective standard
of the reasonable man. A departure from his accustomed sober
behaviour by an act or omission which reveals less than
reasonable care will involve liability at civil law but forms
no basis for the imposition of criminal penalties. In
accordance with well-established principles for the
determination of criminal liability, recklessness, to form a
part of the criminal mens rea, must have an element of the
subjective. It is found in the attitude of one who, aware
that there is danger that his conduct could bring about the
result prohibited by the criminal law, nevertheless
persists, despite the risk. It is, in other words, the
conduct of one who sees the risk and who takes the chance. It
is in this sense that the term "recklessness" is used in the
criminal law and it is clearly distinct from the concept of
civil negligence.

[
30
] He continued at pp. 584-85 S.C.R., pp. 235-36 C.C.C.:

The idea of wilful blindness in circumstances such as this
has been said to be an aspect of recklessness. While this may
well be true, it is wise to keep the two concepts separate
because they result from different mental attitudes and lead
to different legal results. A finding of recklessness in this
case could not override the defence of mistake of fact. The
appellant asserts an honest belief that the consent of the
complainant was not caused by fear and threats. The trial
judge found that such an honest belief existed. In the facts
of this case, because of the reckless conduct of the
appellant, it could not be said that such a belief was
reasonable but, as held in Pappajohn, the mere honesty of the
belief will support the "mistake of fact" defence, even where
it is unreasonable. On the other hand, a finding of wilful
blindness as to the very facts about which the honest belief
is now asserted would leave no room for the application of
the defence because, where wilful blindness is shown, the
law presumes knowledge on the part of the accused, in this
case knowledge that the consent had been induced by threats.

Wilful blindness is distinct from recklessness because,
while recklessness involves knowledge of a danger or risk and
persistence in a course of conduct which creates a risk that
the prohibited result will occur, wilful blindness arises
where a person who has become aware of the need for some
inquiry declines to make the inquiry because he does not wish
to know the truth. He would prefer to remain ignorant. The
culpability in recklessness is justified by consciousness of
the risk and by proceeding in the face of it, while in wilful
blindness it is justified by the accused's fault in
deliberately failing to inquire when he knows there is reason
for inquiry. Cases such as R. v. Wretham
(1971), 16 C.R.N.S.
124 (Ont. C.A.)
; R. v. Blondin (1970),
1970 CanLII 1006 (BC CA)
, 2 C.C.C. (2d) 118,
[1971] 2 W.W.R. 1 (B.C.C.A.); appeal dismissed in this
Court in
1971 CanLII 1411 (SCC)
, 4 C.C.C. (2d) 566n, [1971] S.C.R. v, 1971 CanLII 1411 (SCC), [1972] 1 W.W.R.
479, unreported [no reasons]; R. v. Currie (1975), 24 C.C.C.
(2d) 292 (Ont. C.A.); R. v. McFall et al. (1975),
1975 CanLII 1426 (BC CA)
, 26
C.C.C. (2d) 181 (B.C.C.A.); R. v. Aiello (1978), 38 C.C.C.
(2d) 485,
1978 CanLII 2374 (ON CA)
, 30 N.R. 559 (Ont. C.A.); Roper v. Taylor's
Central Garages (Exeter), Ltd.,
[1951] 2 T.L.R. 284
, among
others illustrate these principles. The text-writers have
also dealt with the subject, particularly Glanville Williams
(Criminal Law: The General Part, 2nd ed. (1961), pp.
157-60). He says, at p. 157:

Knowledge, then, means either personal knowledge or (in the
licence cases) imputed knowledge. In either event there is
someone with actual knowledge. To the requirement of actual
knowledge there is one strictly limited exception. Men
readily regard their suspicions as unworthy of them when it
is to their advantage to do so. To meet this, the rule is
that if a party has his suspicion aroused but then
deliberately omits to make further enquiries, because he
wishes to remain in ignorance, he is deemed to have
knowledge.

[
31
] On this subject, McIntyre J. concluded at p. 586 S.C.R.,
pp. 236-37 C.C.C.:

Glanville Williams, however, warns that the rule of
deliberate blindness has its dangers and is of narrow
application. He says, at p. 159:

The rule that wilful blindness is equivalent to knowledge
is essential, and is found throughout the criminal law. It
is, at the same time, an unstable rule, because judges are
apt to forget its very limited scope. A court can properly
find wilful blindness only where it can almost be said that
the defendant actually knew. He suspected the fact; he
realised its probability; but he refrained from obtaining
the final confirmation because he wanted in the event to be
able to deny knowledge. This, and this alone, is wilful
blindness. It requires in effect a finding that the
defendant intended to cheat the administration of justice.
Any wider definition would make the doctrine of wilful
blindness indistinguishable from the civil doctrine of
negligence in not obtaining knowledge.

This subject is also dealt with by Professor Stuart in
Canadian Criminal Law (1982), p. 130 et seq., where its
relationship to recklessness is discussed.

[
32
] Subsequently, in R. v. Hawkins,
1995 CanLII 85 (SCC)
, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 55, 102
C.C.C. (3d) 97, Sopinka J., on behalf of all members of the
court on the issue of wilful blindness, at p. 110 S.C.R., p.
135 C.C.C., specifically adopted the following passages from
Glanville Williams [Criminal Law: The General Part, 2d ed.,
(London: Stevens & Sons, 1961) at pp. 157-58]:

[T]he rule is that if a party has his suspicion aroused but
then deliberately omits to make further enquiries, because he
wishes to remain in ignorance, he is deemed to have
knowledge.

. . . . .

In other words, there is a suspicion which the defendant
deliberately omits to turn into certain knowledge. This is
frequently expressed by saying that he "shut his eyes" to the
fact, or that he was "wilfully blind".

[
33
] He further adopted, at p. 110 S.C.R., p. 135 C.C.C., the
following passages found at pp. 158-59 of Williams' book:

Before the doctrine of wilful blindness applies, there must
be realisation that the fact in question is probable, or, at
least, "possible above the average."

. . . . .

A court can properly find wilful blindness only where it can
almost be said that the defendant actually knew. He suspected
the fact; he realised its probability; but he refrained from
obtaining the final confirmation because he wanted in the
event to be able to deny knowledge. This, and this alone, is
wilful blindness.

[
34
] Sopinka J. concluded on this issue, at p. 111 S.C.R., p.
135 C.C.C.:

A finding of wilful blindness involves an affirmative
answer to the question: Did the accused shut his eyes because
he knew or strongly suspected that looking would fix him with
knowledge?

[
35
] The Supreme Court returned to the concept of wilful
blindness in R. v. Davis,
1999 CanLII 638 (SCC)
, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 759, 139 C.C.C. (3d)
193. On behalf of the court, Lamer C.J.C. adopted what was said
by McIntyre J. in Sansregret. He stated at pp. 800-01 S.C.R.,
p. 225 C.C.C.:

In R. v. Sansregret,
1985 CanLII 79 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 570 at p. 584, [. . .]
McIntyre J. held that "wilful blindness arises where a person
who has become aware of the need for some inquiry declines to
make the inquiry because he does not wish to know the truth.
He would prefer to remain ignorant." More recently in Esau,
supra, McLachlin J. described wilful blindness as follows at
para. 70:

The term wilful blindness connotes a deliberate avoidance
of the facts and circumstances. It is the legal equivalent
of turning a blind eye, of not seeing or hearing what is
there to hear or see. It is the making of an assumption
that the complainant consents without determining whether,
as a matter of fact, the complainant consents. Blindness as
to the need to obtain consent can never be raised by an
accused as a defence. . . .

(Emphasis in original)

[
36
] I have quoted extensively from the caselaw to make clear
the nature of wilful blindness, as it is now understood, in
order to measure its adequacy to meet the stringent mens rea
requirement for s. 2(b) purposes discussed in Keegstra. In my
opinion, wilful blindness meets the test. As can be seen from
the authorities I have referred to, to be wilfully blind, an
accused must have knowledge of the probability of a fact and
then deliberately refrain from obtaining the final confirmation
in order not to know it. As Glanville Williams aptly put it, it
requires, in effect, a finding that the accused intended to
cheat the administration of justice. I cannot imagine that such
a state of mind could fail to be sufficiently stringent to pass

Charter
muster.

[
37
] The appellant suggested, as a matter of statutory
construction, that the use of the word wilfully in s. 319(2)
itself precludes wilful blindness as a permissible mens rea,
without regard for the
Charter
. Again, I do not agree. As I
indicated above, in Buzzanga, Martin J.A. noted that the word
wilfully has no fixed meaning, and in appropriate cases, can
even include recklessness. While doubt has been cast on this
proposition by the judgment of the Supreme Court in R. v.
Docherty,
1989 CanLII 45 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 941, 51 C.C.C. (3d) 1, there seems to
be little reason to doubt that wilful blindness, being the
equivalent of knowledge, is not excluded from the mens rea of
an offence by the use of the word wilfully. Certainly the use
of the word "knowingly" in an offence-creating provision of the

Criminal Code
does not preclude culpability on the basis of
wilful blindness. (See R. v. Hawkins, supra.)

[
38
] Accordingly, if the trial judge did in fact convict the
appellant on the basis of wilful blindness, I find no error of
law in his doing so. I am convinced that neither
s. 2(b)
of the

Charter
, nor any principle of statutory construction precludes
wilful blindness from being a sufficient mens rea for the
offence created by
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
.

The Meaning and Application of the Defence in
S. 319(3)
(b)

[
39
] Section 319(3)(b) provides that no person shall be
convicted of an offence under s. 319(2) if, in good faith, that
person expressed or attempted to establish by an argument an
opinion on a religious subject. The appellant argues that in
concluding that he was not entitled to the benefit of this
defence the trial judge erred by failing to construe the
defence in accordance with
Charter
values. In particular, he
argues that by isolating certain of Harding's statements from
the rest of his materials, and failing to undertake a
contextual analysis of Harding's expression to determine
whether Harding fell within the purview of the defence, the
trial judge failed to interpret and apply the defence in
accordance with Charter values.

[
40
] It seems clear to me that the learned trial judge did in
fact analyze the passages in the appellant's communications
that he found offensive in context. In fact, in conducting a
contextual analysis, the trial judge concluded that the
appellant's pamphlets and message do contain opinions of
religious belief that he appears to sincerely hold. He also
found, however, that they contained alarming and false
allegations about the adherents of Islam calculated to arouse
fear and hatred of [Muslims] in all non-Muslim people,
particularly Christians. With respect to these allegations, he
stated [at pp. 219-20 O.R.]:

Although expression of religious opinion is strongly
protected, this protection cannot be extended to shield this
type of communication simply because they are contained in
the same message and the one is used to bolster the other. If
that were the case, religious opinion could be used with
impunity as a Trojan Horse to carry the intended message of
hate forbidden by
s. 319
. The intermingling of references to
atrocities being committed by Muslim terrorists abroad, with
Mr. Harding's religious opinions, coupled with his statements
that all Muslims in Canada are the same as those committing
the atrocities, is obviously intended to convey a message
above and beyond religious opinion; that Muslims here are
dangerous and are to be feared.

[
41
] As I have stated, it seems plain to me that the trial
judge did examine the statements of the appellant in context.
He concluded, however, that while the offensive statements were
intermingled with protected religious opinion, they were,
nonetheless, separate false allegations about the adherents of
Islam calculated to arouse fear and hatred of [Muslims] in non-
Muslim people. I see no error in these findings of fact.
Accordingly, unless the defence in
s. 319(3)
(b) is intended to
protect statements that promote hatred against an identifiable
group merely because they are located within a larger statement
that also contains an expression of opinion on a religious
subject, there is no basis to interfere with Linden C.J.C.'s
conclusion that the defence is not available to the appellant.
I see no reason to read
s. 319(3)
(b) as affording such
protection.

[
42
] It seems to me that the plain words of
s. 319(3)
(b) can
only rationally provide a defence to a person who, by
communicating statements other than in private conversation,
wilfully promotes hatred against an identifiable group, in the
rare circumstances where, in the communication of those very
statements, that person, in good faith, was expressing or
attempting to establish by an argument an opinion on a
religious subject. Of course, the trier of fact must look to
the context in order to construe the intention of the maker.
But I see no reason to construe the defence in
s. 319(3)
(b) in
a manner that would permit the mere imbedding of a wilful
message of hate within protected religious comment to immunize
the maker of the message from successful prosecution. As Linden
C. Prov. J. aptly put it, religious opinion could then be used
with impunity as a Trojan horse to carry the intended message
of hate forbidden by
s. 319
.

[
43
] Accordingly, I would not give effect to this ground of
appeal.

The Crown Sentence Appeal

[
44
] I see no basis to interfere with the sentence imposed by
the trial judge, which was carefully crafted to emphasize the
pertinent principles of sentencing, and to fit the
circumstances of this offence and this offender.

Conclusion

[
45
] For the foregoing reasons, both appeals must be
dismissed.

Appeal dismissed.
